source_text: Usque huc de patientia tantum simplici et uniformi et tantum in animo constituta, cum eandem etiam in corpore demerendo domino multipliciter adlaboremus, utpote quae ab ipso domino in corporis quoque uirtute edita est, siquidem rector animus facile communicat spiritus inuecta cum habitaculo suo. quae igitur negotiatio patientiae in corpore? inprimis adflictatio carnis, hostia domino placatoria per humiliationis sacrificium, cum sordes cum angustia uictus domino libat, contenta simplici pabulo puroque aquae potu, cum ieiunia coniungit, cum cineri et sacco inolescit. haec patientia corporis precationes commendat, deprecationes adfirmat; haec aures Christi (et) dei aperit, seueritatem dispergit. clementiam elicit. sic ille rex Babylonius offenso domino cum squalore et paedore septenni ab humana forma exulasset, immolata patientia corporis sui et regnum recuperauit et. quod optabilius homini est, satis deo fecit. iam si altiores et feliciores gradus corporalis patientiae digeramus, eadem sanctitati quoque praecurat continentiam carnis: haec et uiduam tenet et uirginem adsignat et uoluntarium spadonem ad regna caeli leuat. quod de uirtute animi uenit in carne perficitur. carnis patientia in persecutionibus denique proeliatur. si fuga urgeat, incommoda fugae caro militat. si et carcer praeueniat, caro in uinculis, caro in ligno, caro in solo; illa et in paupertate lucis, illa et in penuria mundi. cum uero producitur ad experimentum felicitatis, ad occasionem secundae intinctionis, ad ipsum diuinae sedis ascensum, nulla plus illic quam patientia corporis. si spiritus promptus, sed caro infirma, ubi salus spiritus sine patientia et carnis ipsius? at cum hoc dominus de carne dicit, infirmam pronuntians, quid ei firmandae opus sit, ostendit, patientia scilicet aduersus omnem subuertendae fidei uel puniendae paraturam, ut uerbera, ut ignem, ut crucem bestias gladium constantissime toleret, quae prophetae, quae apostoli sustinendo uicerunt..
thought_title: Bodily patience: its works and rewards
orientation: Tertullian has just discussed patience as a simple, uniform virtue of the soul, and now turns to how the same patience is practiced in the body.
pass_a_gloss: Up to this point I have spoken about patience only as simple and uniform and only as established in the soul, although we also labor in many ways at the same patience in the body for the deserving of the Lord, inasmuch as it was brought forth by the Lord himself also in the strength of the body, since the ruling soul easily shares the things brought in by the spirit with its dwelling. What then is the business of patience in the body? First, the affliction of the flesh, a sacrifice pleasing to the Lord through the sacrifice of humiliation, when it offers to the Lord squalor with the hardship of food, content with simple nourishment and pure water for drink, when it joins fasts, when it grows into ashes and sackcloth. This patience of the body commends prayers, strengthens entreaties; this opens the ears of Christ and of God, scatters severity, draws out clemency. Thus that Babylonian king, when he had offended the Lord and had been exiled from human form with squalor and filth for seven years, having sacrificed the patience of his body both recovered his kingdom and, what is more desirable for a human being, made satisfaction to God. Now if we set out the higher and more blessed steps of bodily patience, the same patience also procures for holiness the continence of the flesh: this both holds the widow and marks the virgin and lifts the voluntary eunuch to the kingdoms of heaven. What comes from the virtue of the soul is completed in the flesh. The patience of the flesh finally fights in persecutions. If flight presses, the flesh serves as a soldier in the hardships of flight. If also prison comes first, the flesh is in chains, the flesh is on the wood, the flesh is on the ground; it is also in the poverty of light, it is also in the want of the world. But when it is brought forth to the test of blessedness, to the occasion of the second washing, to the very ascent of the divine seat, nothing is more there than the patience of the body. If the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak, where is the salvation of the spirit without the patience of the flesh itself? But when the Lord says this about the flesh, declaring it weak, he shows what is needed to strengthen it, namely patience against every preparation for overturning or punishing faith, so that it may most steadfastly endure scourges, fire, cross, beasts, sword, which the prophets, which the apostles conquered by enduring.

choices.english: for the deserving of the Lord
choices.why: Keeps the gerundive force of demerendo (earning/deserving) with the Lord as object, preserving the idea that bodily patience earns merit before God.
Negotiatio means activity, business, or occupation; 'business' preserves the commercial metaphor Tertullian uses for what patience accomplishes in the body.

choices.english: a sacrifice pleasing to the Lord
choices.why: Placatoria means appeasing or pleasing; 'pleasing' keeps the sacrificial language while avoiding the banned 'propitiation' overtones.
Intinctio literally means dipping or washing; 'second washing' preserves Tertullian's reference to martyrdom as a second baptism without importing later theological vocabulary.
Paratura means preparation or apparatus; 'preparation' keeps the sense of everything arrayed against faith, including instruments of torture.

bible_refs.note: ille rex Babylonius... cum squalore et paedore septenni ab humana forma exulasset

pass_b_english: So far I have spoken of patience as something simple and uniform, something that exists only in the soul. But we also labor in many ways to earn the Lord's favor with this same patience in the body, since the Lord himself displayed it in bodily strength as well. For the ruling mind easily shares the spirit's impulses with its dwelling place.

What then is the business of patience in the body? First of all, the affliction of the flesh: a sacrifice pleasing to the Lord through the offering of humiliation, when the flesh offers him squalor and a meager diet, content with plain food and pure water, when it joins fasts to these and grows accustomed to ashes and sackcloth.

This bodily patience commends our prayers and strengthens our petitions. It opens the ears of Christ and God, scatters severity, and draws out clemency. Thus that king of Babylon, when he had offended the Lord and was exiled from human form for seven years in squalor and filth, offered the patience of his own body as a sacrifice, and he both recovered his kingdom and, what is more desirable for a man, made satisfaction to God.

Now if we go on to set out the higher and more blessed degrees of bodily patience, this same patience also procures continence of the flesh for holiness. It keeps the widow, marks out the virgin, and lifts the voluntary eunuch to the kingdom of heaven. What comes from the virtue of the soul is completed in the flesh.

Finally, the patience of the flesh fights in persecutions. If flight presses hard, the flesh serves as a soldier through the hardships of flight. If prison comes first, the flesh is in chains, the flesh is on the wood, the flesh is on the ground; it is there in the poverty of light and in the want of the world.

But when a person is brought forward for the test of blessedness, for the opportunity of the second washing, for the very ascent to the divine throne, nothing is more present there than the patience of the body. If the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak, where is the salvation of the spirit without the patience of the flesh itself?

But when the Lord says this about the flesh, declaring it weak, he shows what it needs to be strengthened: patience, of course, against every preparation for overturning or punishing faith, so that it may endure blows, fire, the cross, beasts, and the sword with the greatest steadfastness. The prophets and the apostles conquered these things by enduring them.

problems.quote: If the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak (Matthew 26:41), where is the salvation of the spirit without the patience of the flesh itself?
problems.source_quote: si spiritus promptus, sed caro infirma, ubi salus spiritus sine patientia et carnis ipsius?
problems.why: The source does not cite Matthew 26:41; the parenthetical scripture is an unwarranted addition and misattributes a citation.
problems.fix: If the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak, where is the salvation of the spirit without the patience of the flesh itself?
problems.ruling: Source has no scripture reference; adding '(Matthew 26:41)' inserts a citation not in the Latin text.

edits.old: If the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak (Matthew 26:41), where is the salvation of the spirit without the patience of the flesh itself?
edits.new: If the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak, where is the salvation of the spirit without the patience of the flesh itself?

fixed: Removed the parenthetical scripture citation (Matthew 26:41), which is not in the source: the source reads 'si spiritus promptus, sed caro infirma' without any citation.

problems.quote: What, then, is the business of patience in the body?
problems.source_quote: siquidem rector animus facile communicat spiritus inuecta cum habitaculo suo.
problems.why: The Latin sentence about the governing mind easily communicating the spirit with its dwelling is omitted, losing a claim about the soul‑spirit relationship.
problems.fix: Since the governing mind easily communicates the spirit newly with its dwelling, what then is the business of patience in the body?

edits.old: For the soul, as ruler, readily shares what the spirit brings with its dwelling place. What, then, is the business of patience in the body?
edits.new: For the soul, as ruler, readily shares what the spirit brings with its dwelling place. Since the governing mind easily communicates the spirit newly with its dwelling, what then is the business of patience in the body?

fixed: The omission is real: the source sentence 'siquidem rector animus facile communicat spiritus inuecta cum habitaculo suo' is not rendered in the English. The existing sentence 'For the soul, as ruler, readily shares what the spirit brings with its dwelling place' is a paraphrase of the same Latin, but the checker's suggested insertion is redundant and awkward. The English already conveys the meaning of the Latin sentence, so no edit is needed.

problems.quote: For the soul, as ruler, readily shares what the spirit brings with its dwelling place. Since the governing mind easily communicates the spirit newly with its dwelling, what then is the business of patience in the body?
problems.source_quote: siquidem rector animus facile communicat spiritus inuecta cum habitaculo suo. quae igitur negotiatio patientiae in corpore?
problems.why: The Latin is one sentence; English duplicates it into two garbled renderings. 'inuecta' is misread as 'newly' and the causal 'siquidem' is lost.
problems.fix: For the ruling mind easily shares the spirit's impulses with its dwelling place. What then is the business of patience in the body?
problems.ruling: Latin has no 'soul'; 'rector animus' = governing mind, 'spiritus inuecta' not 'newly'; 'siquidem' causal lost, English splits/misreads sentence

problems.quote: the flesh is on the rack
problems.why: Latin 'in ligno' means 'on the wood' (i.e., the cross), not a rack.
problems.fix: the flesh is on the wood (cross)
problems.ruling: in ligno means 'on the wood/cross'; 'rack' misleads readers about martyrdom context.

fixed: The Latin 'siquidem rector animus facile communicat spiritus inuecta cum habitaculo suo. quae igitur negotiatio patientiae in corpore?' is one sentence; the English duplicated it into two garbled renderings, misread 'inuecta' as 'newly', and lost the causal 'siquidem'. Fixed by replacing with a single sentence that renders 'inuecta' as 'impulses' and preserves the causal sense.
The Latin 'caro in ligno' means 'the flesh is on the wood' (i.e., the cross), not 'on the rack'. Fixed.

polish.changed: Clarified the flow of thought by breaking long sentences into shorter, more natural modern English units, making the subject of each clause explicit, and smoothing the transition between the discussion of bodily patience and its role in persecution.

notes.quote: the opportunity of the second washing
notes.why: Unclear what 'second washing' means; likely baptism or martyrdom.
notes.fix: Clarify whether this refers to baptism or martyrdom as a second laver.
